title: The marriage contract
hookLine: an ancient document protecting the wife

cards: At a Jewish wedding, under the canopy, there's often a pause. Someone unrolls a document, sometimes painted with flowers and birds and the walls of Jerusalem, and reads it aloud. Guests lean in, expecting poetry.
What they hear, if they follow the old text, sounds more like a bank. Sums of money. Property.
What the husband owes. What happens to her if the marriage ends. Then the document is handed to the bride, and it's hers.
A love story, written as a contract.

teach.h: A PROMISE TO HER, HELD BY HER.
teach.b: Ketubah. Here's what it does. First, it's a promise to her, held by her.
The groom takes on obligations in writing, and the wife keeps the document. The rabbis read a verse in Exodus as saying a husband owes his wife food, clothing and her marital rights.
The ketubah turns that duty into a signed page a court can enforce. Second, it names a sum.
The Mishnah's tractate Ketubot opens with the amounts: two hundred for a woman marrying for the first time, a hundred for a widow. It's money she receives if her husband divorces her or dies.
The rabbis argue over these sums for pages, and the arguing is the point: a wife's future was not to be left to her husband's goodwill. Third, it was made harder to escape.

The Talmud tells of husbands who, when angry, could say: take your ketubah and go. Then Shimon ben Shetach ruled that all of a husband's property stands behind the ketubah. Walking away was no longer cheap.
The contract was a safety net, and a brake. Fourth, it's beautiful anyway.
Over the centuries, Jewish communities turned it into art: illuminated pages, gardens and birds around the legal text, hung on the wall of the couple's home. Today couples choose different texts.
Orthodox couples keep the traditional Aramaic text.
Some Conservative couples add a clause about divorce that you'll hear about soon.
Reform and other couples sometimes write mutual promises in both voices.
Underneath, the same idea: love is real, and so is the day it might fail, and the vulnerable one should not be left with nothing.

how: At a Jewish wedding the ketubah is signed by witnesses, often read aloud under the chuppah, and given to the bride; couples often frame it and hang it in their home. Orthodox couples use the traditional Aramaic text, while Conservative, Reform and other couples may use adapted or mutual texts.

games.q: you're Shimon ben Shetach. husbands are divorcing wives lightly, and the ketubah money is easy to dodge. what do you do?
o: leave it to each husband's conscience.
make all of the husband's property stand behind the ketubah.
lower the sum so more men can pay it.
games.why: the Talmud says he made all of a husband's property liable for the ketubah, so that walking away from her was no longer cheap.

practice: Think of someone who depends on you, or someone you depend on, and ask what protects each of you if things go wrong. Is any of it written down, or is it all goodwill? Just notice; nothing needs fixing in the next two minutes.
